what_it_does: Quantum computers today are in what researchers call the NISQ era (Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum — meaning real devices that have only dozens to a few hundred quantum bits and make frequent errors). Training a Quantum Neural Network (QNN — an AI model whose math runs on quantum hardware instead of a regular chip) across a collection of different quantum devices is hard because those devices vary in their error rates, number of qubits, and availability. Naively treating all devices the same and averaging their results destroys accuracy. ArbiterQ tackles this by giving each quantum device its own personalized model version, described by two compact number-vectors: one capturing the model's learned parameters and one capturing that device's physical behavior. Devices with similar behavior profiles share gradient updates (the small corrections that nudge a model toward better answers during training), so learning is collaborative without being wrecked by devices that behave very differently. A separate scheduling layer then decides how to distribute inference work across available devices to balance load and maintain accuracy, based on how many measurement shots (quantum circuit repetitions needed to get a reliable answer) each device can handle.
